tip: 'Sich erinnern' pairs with 'an' plus accusative: 'an den Namen erinnern' means to remember the name.
'Möchte' (would like) is the polite way to express wants – used much more than 'wollen' in everyday speech.
Formal introductions use 'Ihnen' (dative of 'Sie').
Genitive of masculine and neuter nouns usually adds -s or -es: 'des Projekts' means of the project.
'Dem Kellner' means to the waiter with no separate word for to: the receiver of 'geben' goes dative, and 'dem' carries that to inside it.
'Trauen' takes a dative object: 'seinem eigenen Urteil' (his own judgment).
'Solltest' is Konjunktiv II of 'sollen' – softer, advisory tone.
'War/waren' (was/were) is the Präteritum of 'sein' – one of the few verbs where Präteritum is preferred over Perfekt in speech.
The modal 'könnt' sits in slot 2 and sends its partner verb to the end: 'Ihr könnt das Fahrrad gerne ausleihen'. The infinitive 'ausleihen' closes the clause.
German reverses the miss: 'Das Spielzeug fehlt dem kleinen Mädchen' means the toy is missing to the girl, where English says the girl misses the toy.
English believes the salesman as a direct object, but German gives the person dative: 'Ich glaube dem Verkäufer', not 'den Verkäufer'.
'Dürfen' with 'keine' means forbidden, not 'don't have to': 'dürfen ... keine Pflanzen pflücken' = not allowed to pick any plants.
In a passive, 'by' the doer is 'von', not 'bei' ('bei' would mean at): 'von der Personalabteilung' = by the HR department.
'An' is two-way: staying put takes dative, 'an der Wand' where the picture just hangs there; moving onto it would flip to accusative 'die Wand'.
'Nicht ... sondern' means 'not ... but rather': it rejects one option and swaps in the correction.
'Soll' here conveys a message from someone else – 'I was told to'.
'Hatten' is Präteritum of 'haben' – like 'war', commonly used in speech instead of the Perfekt form.
'Hätte ... gern besucht' is unreal past: she would have liked to attend but did not. Not politeness here, a thing that never happened.
'Sollen' marks an order or expectation coming from someone else, not a personal need. 'Wir sollen leiser sein' = we are told to be quieter.
'Sich beeilen' is reflexive, so it needs the pronoun 'uns'. English hurry has none: 'Wir müssen uns beeilen'.
'Warm' here describes the verb, not a noun, so it takes no ending: 'dich warm anziehen' = to dress warmly.
A modal like 'kann' takes second place and pushes the main verb to the clause end as an infinitive: 'kann ... tippen'.
'Nicht wahr' tacked onto the end is a tag question, like isn't it or right: 'Schönes Wetter heute, nicht wahr?'
After 'das', 'der' or 'die' in the nominative singular, the adjective ends in -e: 'das kalte Wasser'.
After 'ein' with a neuter noun, the adjective takes -es: 'ein kaltes Bier'.
Accusative masculine turns 'ein' into 'einen' and gives the adjective -en: 'einen langen Weg'.
'Gern' has irregular comparison: 'gern', 'lieber', 'am liebsten' (most of all), as in 'Sie trinkt ... am liebsten'.
'Dürfen' means to be allowed to, so 'darfst' signals permission, not ability: 'Du darfst dir ein Eis aussuchen'.
Adding -in makes the female form: 'Mathematiker' becomes 'Mathematikerin'.
Repeated time spans go in the accusative with no preposition: 'jeden Morgen' = every morning.
